name: Rhode Island
summary_text: Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to Rhode Island, because they are issued under national rules rather than state ones. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, new passport applications are processed only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, and passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.  Entry and screening follow the same national layer. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'; the same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. Airport screening carries a separate exposure: the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can reveal a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening of the type matching one's presentation.  Against that background, Rhode Island is listed among the 'Most Protective' states in the anti-trans legal risk assessment published on 13 July 2026, in the gender-identity non-discrimination tier, and the assessment also places Rhode Island among jurisdictions whose shield protections are enforceable against out-of-state action. The same assessment reports erosion at the federal layer and concludes that the top tier can no longer be considered most protective nationwide, so a visitor's protection at the state level coexists with the document, visa and screening rules described above. No Rhode Island-specific restriction on identity documents, facility use or care appears in the source inventory.

name: South Carolina
summary_text: A trans visitor to South Carolina enters under the United States federal document and screening regime before state law applies. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, issuing new passports only as M or F, while previously issued X-marker passports remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.  Entry screening adds exposure. The State Department announced on 25 February 2025 that it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flags visa applicants with an internal marking, and treats a declared gender other than the one assigned at birth as fraud carrying a permanent bar. Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures can involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that risk outing a trans traveller.  Facilities are the sharpest South Carolina-specific exposure. Governor Henry McMaster signed House Bill 4756 into law on 15 May 2026, requiring transgender students in South Carolina public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth. The Senate amended the bill before passage, and the ACLU of South Carolina issued a response on 18 May 2026 framing it as discrimination against trans students in both K-12 and higher education.  The measure extends a pre-existing restriction on school restrooms into campus settings. A July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment, which ranks states on the severity of adult and youth law by reading bills, places South Carolina among the escalating states rather than in the harshest tier.  Custody carries a further state-layer restriction: South Carolina operates a "freeze-frame" policy limiting the treatments transgender inmates may receive while incarcerated. Federal custody is separately affected by the Bureau of Prisons adoption of Florida-based policies for transgender inmates from 2026, which mandate short haircuts, withdrawal of hormone medication and substitution of psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs, and by the Bureau's cessation of reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025.
